\chapter{A Counter for the Shape of the Thing}
\label{ch:ja-counters}
\hlchaptermodality{18}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can put a counter behind a number in Japanese, choose between the general one, the one for people and the one for long thin things, and say which one to reach for when I do not know.}

Complete JA-R18-counting-things: say one thing, one person and one long thin thing, count two eyes, two legs, two people and two hairs, and state the rule with both its edges.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[-tsu]{What the \ja{つ} was doing}

\label{lesson:JA-C18-tsu-counter}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the word for what you have been doing.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{one thing} and \emph{two things} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{eight things} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{six} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} ask for it more slowly, in full — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens — a number cannot stand alone}]
In Japanese a number does not simply sit in front of a thing. It takes a \textbf{counter} — a small word behind the number that says what kind of thing is being counted. Wikipedia's article calls counters \emph{measure words used with numbers to count things, actions, and events}, and English has a few of the same shape: \emph{two \textbf{sheets} of paper}, \emph{three \textbf{head} of cattle}.

You have been using one since chapter nine and nobody said so.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{いちど}} — \emph{ichido} — \textbf{one time}
\end{quote}

Its own lesson said: \emph{ichi is one, and do counts an occurrence.} That \textbf{\ja{ど}} is a counter. It counts occurrences, which is why \textbf{\ja{いちど}} is \emph{one time} and not \emph{one}.

And the \textbf{\ja{つ}} you spent all of last chapter on is a counter too — the \textbf{general} one. That is why nine of the ten native words carry it and \textbf{\ja{とお}} does not.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — when to reach for it}
Japanese has a great many counters and you will not learn them all here. What you can learn in one sentence is the rule that gets you through:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{When you do not know the counter, use the \textasciitilde{}\ja{つ} series.} Up to ten it will carry almost any ordinary object.
\end{quote}

That is exactly what Wikipedia says of the traditional numerals — that the problem of choosing \emph{can often be sidestepped} by using them. \textbf{\ja{ひとつ}} to \textbf{\ja{とお}}, and no further, because that is where the series stops.

\textbf{\ja{コーヒー} \ja{ふたつ}} — two coffees. Nobody will blink.

The rule has an edge, and it is the next lesson: \textbf{people and animals do not take \textasciitilde{}\ja{つ}.} They have counters of their own and there is no way round it.

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Say \textbf{\ja{コーヒー} \ja{ふたつ}}. Then say \textbf{\ja{いちど}} and name the counter inside it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do you use when you do not know the counter? (\textbf{\textasciitilde{}\ja{つ}}, up to ten.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese\_counter\_word}{Wikipedia: Japanese counter word}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E4\%B8\%80\%E3\%81\%A4}{Wiktionary: hitotsu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-nin]{\ja{にん} — counting people}

\label{lesson:JA-C18-nin}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the counter the last rule cannot reach.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say what to use when you do not know the counter — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{の}} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write the small \textbf{\ja{ゅ}} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write the small \textbf{\ja{っ}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{にん}} — \emph{-nin} — the counter for \textbf{people}
\end{quote}

Both signs are old. What is new is that it attaches to the \textbf{borrowed} numbers, not the native ones:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{how many} & \textbf{how you say it} \\
\midrule
three people & \textbf{\ja{さんにん}} \\
four people & \textbf{\ja{よにん}} \\
five people & \textbf{\ja{ごにん}} \\
ten people & \textbf{\ja{じゅうにん}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\ja{さん}} plus \textbf{\ja{にん}}, \textbf{\ja{ご}} plus \textbf{\ja{にん}}. Nothing changes. Four is the one to watch: it is \textbf{\ja{よ}}, not \textbf{\ja{よん}} — the native word again, and shorter here.

You have nine family words and until now no way to say how many of anything you had. \textbf{\ja{こども} \ja{さんにん}} — three children.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens — where the tsu rule stops}]
Last lesson's rule had an edge, and this is it. \textbf{\textasciitilde{}\ja{つ} never counts people.} There is no \emph{hitotsu} of a person; you cannot sidestep \textbf{\ja{にん}}, and the same is true of animals, which have counters of their own.

So the rule now reads with both ends showing: \textbf{use \textasciitilde{}\ja{つ} for ordinary things up to ten; use the proper counter for anything alive.}

And \textbf{\ja{にん}} itself has an exception, at exactly two numbers. That is the next lesson.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Write \textbf{\ja{にん}}. Say \emph{sannin, yonin, gonin, juunin}. Then say \textbf{\ja{こども} \ja{さんにん}}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which number is odd in this list? (\textbf{Four} — \textbf{\ja{よにん}}, not \emph{yonnin}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese\_counter\_word}{Wikipedia: Japanese counter word}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hitori futari]{\ja{ひとり・ふたり} — one person, two people}

\label{lesson:JA-C18-hitori-futari}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the two people the last lesson could not count.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{three people} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nine things} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ten}, then \emph{twelve} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{て}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{ひとり}} — \emph{hitori} — \textbf{one person}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{ふたり}} — \emph{futari} — \textbf{two people}
\end{quote}

Not \emph{ichinin}. Not \emph{ninin}. Every other number takes \textbf{\ja{にん}} and these two do not.

Every sign is yours: \textbf{\ja{ひ}} and \textbf{\ja{ふ}} came two chapters ago, \textbf{\ja{と}}, \textbf{\ja{た}} and \textbf{\ja{り}} long before.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens — the seam, one more time}]
Read the four words together and the exception stops looking like one:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{number} & \textbf{native count} & \textbf{with the people counter} \\
\midrule
one & \textbf{\ja{ひとつ}} & \textbf{\ja{ひとり}} \\
two & \textbf{\ja{ふたつ}} & \textbf{\ja{ふたり}} \\
three & \textbf{\ja{みっつ}} & \textbf{\ja{さんにん}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{hito-} and \emph{futa-} are the same pieces you learned two chapters ago. At one and two, the \textbf{native} number walks into the borrowed counter and stays; from three on, the borrowed number takes over.

That is the third time you have seen this. At \textbf{\ja{よん}} and \textbf{\ja{なな}} the native word stood inside the borrowed count. Here the native word stands inside a borrowed counter. It is one seam, and it runs the whole length of Japanese numbers.

\textbf{\ja{あね} \ja{ひとり、あに} \ja{ふたり}} — one elder sister, two elder brothers.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Write \textbf{\ja{ひとり}} and \textbf{\ja{ふたり}}. Say \emph{hitori, futari, sannin, yonin} — and hear the switch happen between the second and the third.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does the switch happen? (\textbf{Between two and three.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese\_counter\_word}{Wikipedia: Japanese counter word}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Counting your own face}

\label{lesson:JA-C18-count-the-face}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the first thing in this book you can count.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{one person} and \emph{two people} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{face} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{た}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn — count what you have}
Chapter twelve gave you a face. Until this chapter you could name every part of it and say how many of nothing.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{め} \ja{ふたつ}} — two eyes
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{みみ} \ja{ふたつ}} — two ears
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{はな} \ja{ひとつ}} — one nose
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{くち} \ja{ひとつ}} — one mouth
\end{quote}

Four nouns, none of them alive on its own, so the \textbf{\textasciitilde{}\ja{つ}} rule covers all four without your having to know a thing about which counter a nose takes.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the four face lines without stopping, then \textbf{\ja{ふたり}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the four needed you to know a special counter? (\textbf{None.}) Which nearby word did? (\textbf{A person} — \textbf{\ja{ふたり}}, not \textbf{\ja{ふたつ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ho]{\ja{ほ} — \ja{は} with one more bar}

\label{lesson:JA-W18-ho}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the last sign of the chapter.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} count the four parts of a face — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{ひ}} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{だ}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{ほ}} — \emph{ho}
\end{quote}

Write \textbf{\ja{は}} first. You have had it since chapter one: a left vertical, one horizontal, then the right stroke that loops at the foot.

\textbf{\ja{ほ}} is that figure with \textbf{one more horizontal}, and Sirgazil's animation puts it above the one \textbf{\ja{は}} already has. Four strokes, in this order:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item the left vertical, hooking at the foot
  \item the \textbf{upper} horizontal on the right
  \item the \textbf{lower} horizontal on the right
  \item the right vertical, down through both bars and looping at the foot
\end{enumerate}

So the only thing you are learning is a bar, and where it goes.

\textbf{\ja{ほ}} also finishes a set. Japanese's \textbf{h-row} runs \emph{ha, hi, fu, he, ho}, and you now hold four of its five: \textbf{\ja{は}} from chapter one, \textbf{\ja{ひ}} and \textbf{\ja{ふ}} from two chapters ago, and \textbf{\ja{ほ}} here. Only \textbf{\ja{へ}} is missing.

Write \textbf{\ja{ひ}} once beside them and hear the row.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Write \textbf{\ja{は}}, then \textbf{\ja{ほ}} beneath it, and mark the stroke that differs.
  \item Copy \textbf{\ja{ほ}}; hide it; write it again.
  \item Say both aloud: \emph{ha}, \emph{ho}. Then say \textbf{\ja{ひとつ}} and hear the same \textbf{\ja{ひ}}.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many strokes? (\textbf{Four.})

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U3040.pdf}{Unicode Hiragana chart}; stroke count and order per \href{https://kanjivg.tagaini.net/kanjivg/kanji/0307b.html}{KanjiVG} and Sirgazil's Commons animation.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-hon]{\ja{ほん} — counting long thin things}

\label{lesson:JA-C18-hon}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then a counter chosen by shape.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{ほ}} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hand} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say what \textasciitilde{}\ja{つ} is for, and what it is not for — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{ほん}} — \emph{-hon} — the counter for \textbf{long, thin things}
\end{quote}

Wikipedia's list for it is worth reading whole: \emph{rivers, roads, train tracks, ties, pencils, bottles, guitars.} Nothing on that list is a book, though the sign it is written with is \textbf{\ja{本}} — the very kanji you have been writing since chapter five, inside \textbf{\ja{日本語}}.

That is the shape rule in one word: \textbf{\ja{ほん}} does not care what the thing \emph{is}, only that it is longer than it is wide.

Two of your own words qualify. One of them you can already say:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{あし} \ja{にほん}} — two legs
\end{quote}

The other is \textbf{\ja{かみ}}, a hair — and the word for \emph{one} hair has to wait two lessons, because at one the counter changes shape.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens — the counter bends the sound}]
\textbf{\ja{にん}} attached to the numbers and nothing moved. \textbf{\ja{ほん}} does not behave. Here are the four that leave it alone:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{number} & \textbf{the form} \\
\midrule
two & \textbf{\ja{にほん}} \\
four & \textbf{\ja{よんほん}} \\
five & \textbf{\ja{ごほん}} \\
seven & \textbf{\ja{ななほん}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

At \textbf{three} the \textbf{\ja{ほ}} takes the \textbf{dakuten} you have had since chapter three, and at \textbf{one, six, eight and ten} it goes further still — further than the dakuten can take it. Both of those need a mark on the sign, and the second mark is one this book has never taught. The next two lessons buy it and then spend it; until then, say the four plain ones.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Write \textbf{\ja{ほん}}. Say \emph{nihon, yonhon, gohon, nanahon} — the four that leave the counter alone. Then say \textbf{\ja{あし} \ja{にほん}}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ja{ほん}} count? (\textbf{Anything longer than it is wide.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese\_counter\_word}{Wikipedia: Japanese counter word}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[handakuten]{\ja{゜} — the other mark}

\label{lesson:JA-W18-handakuten}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the mark the last lesson stopped short of.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{three long thin things} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{ふ}}, all four strokes — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ear} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{゜}} — the \textbf{handakuten}
\end{quote}

A small circle, written at the top right of a kana, in the same place the \textbf{dakuten} goes.

Japanese has exactly two of these marks and you have had one of them since chapter three:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{mark} & \textbf{what it does} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ja{゛}} dakuten & voices the consonant & \textbf{\ja{ほ}} $\to$ \textbf{\ja{ぼ}} \\
\textbf{\ja{゜}} handakuten & turns the \textbf{h}-row into \textbf{p} & \textbf{\ja{ほ}} $\to$ \textbf{\ja{ぽ}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The handakuten works on \textbf{one row only} — the row \textbf{\ja{は}} and \textbf{\ja{ほ}} belong to. Nowhere else in the syllabary does it appear, which makes it the rarest thing in the writing system and the easiest to place: if you see the little circle, the sign under it is an h-row kana and the sound is \textbf{p}.

That row is the one you have just been filling in. \textbf{\ja{ふ}} takes both marks too, giving \emph{bu} and \emph{pu}, and so does \textbf{\ja{は}}. The mark is rare; the row is not.

Write the circle small. It is a circle, not a dot, and it does not touch the sign it sits on.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Write \textbf{\ja{ほ}}, then \textbf{\ja{ぼ}}, then \textbf{\ja{ぽ}}, and say all three.
  \item Say the same three sounds on \textbf{\ja{は}}, without writing them.
  \item Check one thing: is the circle open?
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which row does the handakuten work on? (\textbf{Only the h-row.})

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U3040.pdf}{Unicode Hiragana chart}, U+309C.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ippon]{\ja{いっぽん} — and the four that bend}

\label{lesson:JA-C18-ippon}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the form the counter takes at one.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{ぽ}} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mouth} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write the small \textbf{\ja{っ}} — \textbf{R2}, six lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{いっぽん}} — \emph{ippon} — \textbf{one long thin thing}
\end{quote}

Not \emph{ichihon}. The \textbf{\ja{いち}} shortens to \textbf{\ja{いっ}}, and the \textbf{\ja{ほ}} takes the handakuten you learned last lesson.

Here is the whole counter, with the numbers this book can spell:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{number} & \textbf{the form} & \textbf{what happens} \\
\midrule
one & \textbf{\ja{いっぽん}} & \textbf{p}, and a held beat \\
two & \textbf{\ja{にほん}} & plain \\
three & \textbf{\ja{さんぼん}} & \textbf{b} \\
four & \textbf{\ja{よんほん}} & plain \\
five & \textbf{\ja{ごほん}} & plain \\
six & \textbf{\ja{ろっぽん}} & \textbf{p}, and a held beat \\
seven & \textbf{\ja{ななほん}} & plain \\
eight & \textbf{\ja{はっぽん}} & \textbf{p}, and a held beat \\
ten & \textbf{\ja{じゅっぽん}} & \textbf{p}, and a held beat \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Nine is missing from that table on purpose.} Its everyday form needs a sign this book has not taught, so it is left out rather than guessed at.

Read the shape of the rest: \textbf{one, six, eight and ten} all end in a held beat and take \textbf{p}. \textbf{Three} ends in the nasal \textbf{\ja{ん}} and takes \textbf{b}. Everything else is plain. The counter is not being irregular — it is being pushed by the sound in front of it.

\textbf{\ja{かみ} \ja{いっぽん}} — one hair.

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Write \textbf{\ja{いっぽん}}. Say the run: \emph{ippon, nihon, sanbon, yonhon, gohon, roppon}. Then say \textbf{\ja{かみ} \ja{いっぽん}}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why is nine missing from the table? (\textbf{Its form needs a sign this book has not taught.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese\_counter\_word}{Wikipedia: Japanese counter word}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Three counters, and how to choose}

\label{lesson:JA-R18-counting-things}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the run.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{one long thin thing} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{three things} and \emph{four things} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nose} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{leg} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say what to use when you do not know the counter — \textbf{R2}, nine lessons back
\end{itemize}

Nothing new arrives here.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn — the run}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\ja{かみ} \ja{いっぽん}}, \textbf{\ja{あし} \ja{にほん}}, \textbf{\ja{ふたり}}, \textbf{\ja{はな} \ja{ひとつ}}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\ja{ほ}}, then the same sign with the handakuten — \textbf{\ja{ぽ}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
A number in Japanese does not stand on its own. It takes a \textbf{counter}, and the counter is chosen by what kind of thing is being counted:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the thing} & \textbf{the counter} \\
\midrule
an ordinary object, up to ten & \textbf{\textasciitilde{}\ja{つ}} \\
a person & \textbf{\ja{にん}} \\
anything longer than it is wide & \textbf{\ja{ほん}} \\
an occurrence & \textbf{\ja{ど}}, which you had in chapter nine \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both edges of that are worth carrying. \textbf{Reach for \textasciitilde{}\ja{つ} when you do not know} — up to ten it will carry almost any ordinary object. \textbf{Do not reach for it for anything alive}, and do not expect it past ten.

And the seam this book has been drawing since chapter fourteen runs through all of it. \textbf{\ja{よん}} and \textbf{\ja{なな}}: the native word inside the borrowed count. \textbf{\ja{ひとり}} and \textbf{\ja{ふたり}}: the native word inside a borrowed counter. Two counts, and the places where they touch are not random — they are the same handful of numbers, every time.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do you use when you do not know the counter? (\textbf{\textasciitilde{}\ja{つ}}, to ten.) Where does that rule fail? (\textbf{Anything alive.}) Say one person and one hair. (\textbf{\ja{ひとり}}; \textbf{\ja{かみ} \ja{いっぽん}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
